transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ruben Ortiz (Redwood SE), Tom Ellis (CTO, Fenwick), Priya Nair (ML Lead), Ahmed Khan (Head Infra), Liam (PM)

Summary: short discovery where Fenwick wants an "escape hatch" from their current hosted provider for both cost reasons and to enable private hosting for regulated customers. They run a mix of low-latency chat and large-batch analysis pipelines (vLLM locally).

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for taking the time, can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Tom: yep, good here. thanks Maya.
[00:08] Maya: cool, quick intros — im Maya, AE on this account, Ruben our solutions engineer will run through technical fit. you can do quick care of roles?
[00:15] Tom: im Tom, CTO, i look after infra decisions.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, ML lead, i own the model evals and prompt sets.
[00:22] Ahmed: Ahmed, infra, network and security.
[00:25] Liam: Liam - product PM, here for success criteria.
[00:29] Ruben: hey all. thanks.

[02:05] Maya: quick overview - Redwood offers hosted api, dedicated reserved pools, and private vpc/on-prem options. common for folks migrating off OpenAI/Anthropic or using vLLM/TGI locally. im curious where you are today?
[02:20] Tom: we currently use a hosted provider for most chat, cost started spiking. for heavy offline workloads we run v l m in-house — it's working but ops heavy. we need a path that gives parity at inference quality and lower unit cost with better control.
[02:40] Priya: and we have strict data residency for a subset of customers, so VPC or onprem is must for those.

[04:12] Ruben: got it. when you say parity - what metrics do you look at? is it token-level perplexity or human eval?
[04:20] Priya: mixture. we have golden outputs for a set of prompts and also human evals for hallucination and answer correctness. latency is important for our chat UI — 95th percentile under ~150-200ms for short conversations. batch jobs care about throughput and cost.

[06:45] Maya: okay makes sense. couple of tradeoffs to call out — hosted gives fastest time-to-value, dedicated gives predictable throughput and capacity isolation and we'd recommend private if you need full network control and customer-managed keys.
[07:05] Tom: curious on the effort to get model parity — you guys support TGI formats and vllm kernels?
[07:15] Ruben: yes, we onboard model variants. we've got a model catalog and runtime that supports common formats — we do kernel selection and quantization profiles. sometimes there are gotchas with kv cache handling across implementations which can change latencies and outputs slightly, so we usually run an eval parity sprint.
[07:45] Priya: that kv cache comment - can you expand? we saw differences between our in-house v l m and open hosted provider, sometimes responses truncate or the context window behaves slightly different.
[08:00] Ruben: sure - kv cache management, prompt chunking, and past key-value handling across attention optimizations can shift token alignments. we log token-level diffs and run a sniff test for functional parity. often the model weights are the same but serving primitives differ.

[10:30] Ahmed: on security — we need SOC2, single-tenant options for certain customers, and KMS/HSM for keys. is that supported?
[10:38] Maya: yes — SOC2 report available, KMS integrations supported for Dedicated and Private, HSM notes in the security pack. audit logs and request-level tracing are in Console. i'll send the pack.

[12:50] Liam: pricing — rough order of magnitude? we have heavy bursty usage.
[12:55] Maya: rough numbers on token unit cost vary by model. hosted is usage-based billed monthly; dedicated is reserved commit with lower unit cost and predictable throughput. for your burst patterns we might recommend a dedicated pool with burst capacity. we'll send an options spreadsheet.

[14:30] Tom: performance wise, how do you measure latency SLOs? and what about canaries and fallback to cheaper model variants?
[14:42] Ruben: we surface token-level latency, per-route SLOs, and automatic fallback policies. you can route by latency or cost. for example if a high-cost model is unavailable we can fallback to a quantized variant automatically — with configured rollback on quality regression.

[17:10] Priya: for eval parity — what's the typical cadence and output of a sprint?
[17:17] Ruben: usually we run a 1-2 week sprint: 1) you give us prompt set + golden outputs 2) we run on hosted and dedicated/private test environments, gather diffs (token diffs, rouge/bleu-ish metrics, plus human spot checks), 3) produce a report with recommended quantization or minor prompt changes. will also include latency/throughput numbers.

[20:05] Ahmed: networking — for a VPC private deployment, do you support VPC peering and transit gateways? any constraints on egress?
[20:15] Maya: yes, we support VPC peering and private link options with on-prem connectors. egress patterns depend on deployment mode — in private we aim for customer-controlled egress. we'll note specifics in the infra diagram.

[23:40] Tom: we have a subset of customers in EU requiring data residency. can Redwood limit model outputs/logs staying in-region?
[23:50] Ruben: yes, we can pin regions and we support per-tenant retention policies and regionally siloed logs for Private/Dedicated. hosted can be region-limited but private gives more control.

[27:00] Priya: tokenization differences sometimes cause drift — e.g. one provider's tokenizer inserts unseen special tokens on certain sequences. do you normalize tokenizers?
[27:12] Ruben: we usually run tokenizer alignment checks as part of parity. if needed we apply pre-tokenization steps or a tokenizer shim to match behavior.

[30:30] Liam: plan for pilot?
[30:35] Maya: propose next: we send security pack, Ruben will share a benchmark template. you (Priya) send a 50-100 prompt subset and golden outputs, we run a 1-hour benchmark on Hosted and Dedicated test pool and share results — that should show parity and perf.
[31:00] Tom: perfect. timeline? next week?
[31:05] Maya: yes, aim for next Tue/Wed — Ruben, is that realistic?
[31:10] Ruben: yep i can carve out a slot for bench run and bring logging hooks.

[33:20] Priya: one more — we use a custom reranker and embeddings pipeline, will Redwood preserve existing vector indexes or do we need to re-embed?
[33:30] Ruben: embeddings compatibility depends on model family. we support common embeddings; for private/dedicated you can bring your index, but often we recommend reembedding with recommended model for better alignment — we can run a migration plan for embeddings too.

[36:45] Ahmed: backup question — if we start with hosted and later want private, how smooth is the migration? downtime?
[36:55] Maya: migration path is designed to be incremental — same API surface and rollout policies. usually it's blue/green or canary rollouts; minimal downtime if planned. there are infra steps for VPC peering and key handoff that take coordination.

[40:10] Tom: anything else we should be aware of on cost or hidden overhead?
[40:16] Ruben: watch for cross-region egress and long context window costs; KV caching and batching settings can materially impact cost. we can provide quantization recommendations and batching configs to reduce per-token spend while meeting latency.

[43:50] Priya: ok action items — we'll put together the prompt set and token distribution, Ahmed will check VPC constraints.
[44:05] Maya: great — i'll send SOC2, KMS docs and the pricing options. Ruben will share the benchmark template.
[45:30] Liam: schedule follow-up after bench.
[46:10] Tom: thanks all.
[46:15] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark. bye.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts: "v l m" appears for vLLM, "T G I" for TGI, some names mis-attributed in auto transcript.
